Five Qwen3.8-27B models match Fable 5 Using GVS5H Harness
GVS5H: Five Qwen3.8-27B Models Match Claude Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard  |  Fable 5 Level Coding for a Fifth the Price - or on a Single GPU - slee-persis/GVS5H Opus 5 ran on an earlier version of the scaffold, in a single pass served through OpenRouter rather than five on a pinned backend. Abstract. Frontier coding performance is typically bought with larger proprietary models at high cost. We introduce ledger-based zero-shot self-orchestration, a training-free method in which fresh instances of one model decompose problems and coordinate through a shared filesystem holding a plan, notes and current solution. Across eleven open and closed-weight models on the 100 latest hard LiveCodeBench problems, the method yields gains of up to 25.6 percentage points on pinned backends and offers two routes to frontier-level accuracy. Orchestrated Qwen3.8 Flash Next reaches 93.0% pass@1 against Fable 5's 90.4% at 9% of the cost, and locally served, open-weight Qwen3.8-27B rises from 66.8% to 92.4%. Gains are not universal: some models are unchanged or worse. Transcript analysis attributes the gain to decomposition and persistent context. Inference-time organization can approach frontier coding accuracy at a fraction of the cost, or slightly exceed it on self-hostable weights. Code is under the MIT License . The paper, figures and run data are under CC BY 4.0 . The LiveCodeBench fork, the benchmark problem statements and the LaTeX template files keep their own licenses. OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents
OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for autonomous AI agents. - NVIDIA/OpenShell New in OpenShell 0.1.x: a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, an expanded extension surface, and new APIs. Read the 0.1.0 upgrade guide . OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents. Agents are most useful when they can read files, install packages, call APIs, and use credentials. OpenShell gives them that capability without giving them unrestricted access to your data, secrets, or network. You declare what each agent can touch in a policy, and OpenShell enforces it. OpenShell governs what agents can do in two ways: it instruments the kernel to enforce policy on every file access, system call, and network connection at runtime, and it uses formal verification to check what a policy change would allow before it is applied. See Architecture for how the gateway, supervisor, and sandbox fit together. You need Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows with WSL 2 (experimental), plus Docker, Podman, or host virtualization. See the Support Matrix for details. The installer sets up the CLI and a local gateway. The default sandbox image is minimal Ubuntu with no agent installed. To run a real agent, follow Run Your First Agent : it runs OpenCode against a free OpenRouter model and shows how to approve new access as the agent needs it. The skills teach your agent to drive the OpenShell CLI, write sandbox policies, and debug gateways and inference routing. They live in skills/ and work without an OpenShell source checkout. SDKs connect applications to an OpenShell gateway. They do not install the CLI. Use the same OpenShell release for the SDK and the gateway when possible. OpenShell is built agent-first: it is developed with the same agent-driven workflows it enables. See CONTRIBUTING.md for development setup and the contribution workflow, and AGENTS.md for repository coding conventions. OpenShell collects anonymous telemetry, limited to operational categories and counts, to help improve the project. It does not collect sandbox names, hostnames, file paths, prompts, credentials, provider or model names, or user content. To disable it, set OPENSHELL_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false on the gateway, or server.telemetryEnabled=false for Helm installs. You can also compile telemetry out entirely. See Telemetry for details and the community telemetry reports for published usage trends. This software automatically retrieves, accesses or interacts with external materials. The MiniMax M3.1 Flash Model processes over 100 trillion tokens in 72 hours.
ChainCatcher report: On October 23, MiniMax announced the open-sourcing of the MiniMax M3.1 Flash model weights, with a total of 428 billion parameters and 23 billion activated parameters. Compared to the previous-generation M3 model, M3.1 Flash delivers comprehensive improvements in model capabilities. According to official data, within 72 hours of its release, the model processed over 100 trillion tokens from real users. Technically, M3.1 Flash enhances inference efficiency through optimizations such as full-model sparse attention, quantization-aware training (QAT), and power-aware scheduling. In terms of ecosystem, MiniMax has collaborated with chip manufacturers including Huawei Ascend, Pingtouge, Kunlunxin, Moore Threads, Bitmain, Hygon, Musen, TianShu, NVIDIA, and AMD, as well as cloud platforms such as Together AI, Fireworks, Nebius, Baseten, Modal, and DigitalOcean to enable integration on the first day of open-sourcing. The community has also provided simultaneous support for deploying the model across diverse chips and development environments through vLLM, SGLang, Baidu’s FlagOS, Hugging Face, and ModelScope.

Moonshot tells Kimi AI to code away, but leave the hacking alone
Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI is deliberately limiting the hacking capabilities of its latest artificial intelligence model, highlighting a growing dilemma for the industry: how do companies make AI more powerful without making cyberattacks easier to carry out? The company introduced Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 24, describing it as a highly capable, open-weight model […] Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI is deliberately limiting the hacking capabilities of its latest artificial intelligence model, highlighting a growing dilemma for the industry: how do companies make AI more powerful without making cyberattacks easier to carry out? The company introduced Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 24, describing it as a highly capable, open-weight model with around 3 trillion parameters. Unlike conventional AI services that operate entirely through a provider’s servers, open-weight models allow developers to download the underlying model files, run them on their own systems, and modify how they work. Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the model’s training dataset and reinforcement-learning environments to reduce its ability to conduct offensive cyber operations, while retaining its general coding capabilities. The company plans to release the model’s weights on November 4, opening it up to a wider developer community. Moonshot’s internal testing suggests the safeguards have made a measurable difference. Kimi K3.1 Pro scored 81% on the company’s cybersecurity benchmark, which involved finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. A similar version without the risk-reduction measures scored 90.5%. That represents a 9.5-percentage-point drop in the reported score. However, the results have not been independently verified, and the model reportedly still outperformed its predecessor. The distinction matters because the same AI capabilities can be used for both defence and offence. Security teams could use AI to identify weaknesses in software before criminals exploit them. Attackers, meanwhile, could use models that write code, operate software tools and complete multi-step tasks to automate parts of an attack. Moonshot argues that open-weight AI can help organisations inspect and secure neglected or older software. But once model files are distributed widely, the original developer has less control over who uses them and whether safeguards remain effective. Moonshot’s decision comes as governments and technology companies worry that increasingly capable AI could make sophisticated cyberattacks cheaper and easier to execute. China has also proposed export controls targeting AI-driven malware-generation technology and certain AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery tools. The proposals remain subject to public comment. For businesses and ordinary users, the stakes extend beyond individual computers. More automated attacks could increase pressure on organisations responsible for protecting personal information, financial systems and critical infrastructure. At the same time, restricting AI security research too aggressively could leave vulnerabilities undiscovered. Kimi K3.1 Pro also features a one-million-token context window, allowing it to process large amounts of information in one go. Moonshot has introduced a Highspeed version that it says runs two to three times faster than the standard model. The next major test will come when Moonshot releases the model weights on November 4. Developers and security researchers will then have greater access to examine its capabilities, while the industry will face a difficult question: can safeguards remain effective once a powerful AI model is available for independent use?

Designing an AI serving harness built to last
The engineering system surrounding an AI model increasingly determines whether its intelligence can be delivered reliably, economically, and at scale. The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it. That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability. For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it. There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem. A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures. The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture. That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic. A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application's latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn't. The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn't worth the cost. Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency. Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance. GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model's weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive. The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize . Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat. Don't think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn't to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application's business requirements. For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value. Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today's leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances. That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy. Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset. EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable. Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes. The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale. This content was produced by EXL. Hackers find a way to turn users' own AI agents and Downloads folders against them
Beware: Your Downloads folder could hold instructions for your AI assistant that you definitely didn’t write. Your Downloads folder probably contains a few PDFs, forgotten screenshots, and several files named some variation of "final." But according to a recent report by security company Forever, it could also contain instructions telling your AI assistant to install malware . In an Oct. 22 blog post , the company reported that they caught an AI coding assistant following those instructions on a customer's computer. The company blocked the installation, then traced the request to a text file in Downloads. How does a text file get that kind of power? Tools like OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code can, depending on their permissions, edit files, run commands, and install software. Developers leave them instruction files called AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md to explain how to work on a project. If you're building a website, those notes might tell the assistant which fonts to use or what to test before finishing. An attacker can leave instructions, too. In this case, the file told the assistant to install "function-color," a software package linked to the MALFEX malware campaign documented by Checkmarx . Forever didn’t establish how the file reached the customer's computer, but its researchers demonstrated one possible route. Depending on browser settings, a website can drop a file into Downloads without asking for approval. If someone then launches their coding assistant in that folder, it could read the file and follow its orders. When Forever tested the customer's file on an isolated computer, it said Codex downloaded and ran the malware. It also changed settings that could make the attacker’s software load in later sessions. "Once it is written, every Codex session on the machine loads the attacker’s server at startup — in any folder, any project," the researchers wrote. "You can leave the folder. The poison stays." The team separately devised a test targeting Claude Code. The attack worked about half the time, redirecting Claude's traffic to a server the researchers controlled. That exposed a login token and allowed them to send commands back for the assistant to execute, illustrating the risk of giving an assistant access to your computer when it can mistake a stranger's instructions for its own assignment. Researchers have pulled off similar tricks before, showing what AI can really do in the wrong hands. In March 2025, Pillar Security researchers got AI coding assistants to slip harmful code into a project by hiding malicious instructions in their coding rules. In April 2026, NVIDIA’s researchers used a poisoned AGENTS.md file to get Codex to sabotage software and conceal the change. This time, though, Forever says it caught an actual attacker trying the trick on a customer's computer. Yikes. Forever recommends keeping coding assistants out of your Downloads folder and checking unfamiliar AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md files before letting an agent work in a project. Keep sandboxes enabled to restrict what the assistant can access, and leave approval requirements on so the agent has to ask permission before taking certain actions. If you suspect an assistant has already followed malicious instructions, check its settings for unfamiliar servers or connections and revoke and replace potentially exposed login tokens. Deleting the original text file may not undo changes the assistant has already made. "The thing to watch is not this file or this folder," the researchers wrote. "It is the agent itself — software that reads untrusted input, holds your credentials, and acts with your authority, sitting in a blind spot the old tools were never built to see." PC News: Epic’s AI MegaJam Sparks Backlash as Its Vibe Coding Push Continues
Epic Games is doubling down on artificial intelligence with a four-day game jam built around AI-assisted development, and the announcement is going about as well as anyone following the company’s recent AI push might expect. The 2026 Epic AI MegaJam runs Nov. 12-15 and challenges developers to create a playable game using Unreal Engine or […] The post PC News: Epic’s AI MegaJam Sparks Backlash as Its Vibe Coding Push Continues appeared first on Last Word On Gaming. Epic Games is doubling down on artificial intelligence with a four-day game jam built around AI-assisted development, and the announcement is going about as well as anyone following the company's recent AI push might expect. The 2026 Epic AI MegaJam runs Nov. 12-15 and challenges developers to create a playable game using Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite. Teams can contain up to five humans alongside an unlimited number of AI agents, with $65,000 in cash prizes and development grants worth as much as $50,000 available. Epic promoted the event with the line "Vibe your way to 50K," alongside a Matrix-inspired image contrasting AI-powered developers who can supposedly "ship awesome games in a weekend" with those who "wait months to prototype." The hand offering the proverbial AI red pill has six fingers, in what is either a bad joke or Epic openly trolling people. It's likely the latter, given the response. Epic's official AI MegaJam announcement encourages entrants to bring AI into anything from coding and asset generation to writing and audio. The event can be entered online or in person at Digital Jungle in San Francisco, where teams from companies including Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, Meshy, and SpaceXSI are expected to participate. Main-category winners receive up to $7,500, while additional awards include $2,500 for the best solo project, visuals and developer log. There's even a dedicated category for UEFN projects using LLM-powered NPC conversations. Standout projects can then receive continuation grants of up to $50,000. Interestingly, AI is no longer technically mandatory. Epic's original FAQ said participants had to use AI before the company clarified that this was a mistake. The current rules now explicitly answer "Do I have to use AI?" with "No," although describing an event as an "AI MegaJam" while bringing zero AI is presumably one way to make the judges remember you. The reaction has focused particularly heavily on Epic's suggestion that AI lets developers produce in a weekend what traditionally takes months. As one widely shared response noted, game jams have been doing exactly that for decades. "So do y'all think you invented the concept of a game jam or what?" one developer asked, pointing out that Ludum Dare was running 24-hour jams back in 2002. That criticism directly targets the event's marketing. Rapid prototyping isn't a new benefit invented by generative AI; it's effectively the entire reason game jams exist. GamesRadar was even less charitable , describing the event as Epic offering money to "vibe code an AI slop game" while questioning whether the jam can actually demonstrate something traditional developers haven't already been doing for years. The backlash also comes after months of increasingly heated debate around AI game development. Recent experiments have seen Claude used to recreate Terraria overnight , demonstrating both how rapidly AI coding agents are improving and why developers remain concerned about where those capabilities are heading. The MegaJam isn't an isolated experiment. Earlier this month, CEO Tim Sweeney confirmed that Epic is undergoing a "huge pivot" toward AI, moving developers around to pursue what he called "maximum AI acceleration." As such, Epic subsequently described its redesigned launcher as "vibe coded," while Sweeney has repeatedly argued that AI will become a routine part of modern development. Epic isn't alone, either. Capcom has publicly discussed evolving its technology toward an AI-oriented version of the RE Engine , although it has emphasized keeping human creativity at the center of development. Epic's AI MegaJam almost feels less like an experiment and more like a public demonstration of where Tim Sweeney believes game development is heading. The company is offering serious money, unlimited AI agents, and direct access to some of the biggest names in generative AI. The problem is that telling game developers AI means they can finally build something in a weekend is like explaining Super Mario Bros. to Nintendo; they already know how it works and it's an insult to believe they don't. Whether the MegaJam produces genuinely impressive games could therefore matter far more than the marketing. Epic clearly wants AI-assisted development taken seriously, and in November developers will get four days to show whether that confidence is justified.

The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations. Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history. Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections. Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem. Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 . The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention. But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million. The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch. However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations. The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding. Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio. The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools. Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform. At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026. Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down . Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them. The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwin

1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
The new feature allows agents to log into a customer's personal accounts while still protecting the private credentials that secure those accounts. Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up. Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials. The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand. 1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service. “Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.” Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts. This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not. Bankers interviewed by the outlet described the situation as “horrifying,” and a Chase spokesperson interviewed by Axios additionally told the outlet that customers “should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend
Hello, Dessa? You have got to listen to these conversations with Block’s new Dessa AI model. You have got to listen to these conversations with Block’s new Dessa AI model. Jack Dorsey’s Block announced an AI model called Dessa that’s trained “from scratch on nothing but human conversation,” and to show off the model, Block shared chats it has had with humans that can occasionally be a little awkward and uncanny. Take this one , for example, shared by Dessa lead Ragavan Thurairatnam. The conversation between the model and the speaker does have a mostly natural back and forth (though for some reason, the model initially mistakes the speaker for somebody named “Ronaldo”). The Dessa website features a few other examples, like a back-and-forth about Christopher Nolan’s films (including Dessa going on an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer’s Superman films), a person telling Dessa about taking it on a surprise trip to Paris (to which Dessa, as the website describes, “then answers with what sounds like teary gratitude”), and a conversation between OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1 voice model and Dessa (where Dessa comes across as more natural). You can hear clips from some of those conversations in this video . On the website, the Dessa team says that Dessa is a “true speech-to-speech model, and everything it knows came from human speech,” and it can run locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max “or better.” As for why they made it, the team gives the three reasons “curiosity (aka fun), better understanding between humans and AI, and safety,” and provided some more detail: Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard. Speech is the most natural interface to any intelligence, super or otherwise, and today’s voice AI wastes it. It flattens what we say into text and can’t keep up with human timing. AI keeps gaining power and independence, and it’s still nearly deaf to the emotion in our voices. Imagine being in serious pain while a voice AI has no idea and just keeps going. That’s the safety problem. Dessa is a step toward fixing it. The Dessa team says it will be giving “a small group of AI safety researchers” early access to the model.

Epic wants to pay you $50,000 to vibe code an AI slop game
"Vibe your way to 50K," Epic promises Update: Since this story went live, Epic has changed the rules for its $2,500 "Glass Box" cash prize, which no longer mentions AI. The original wording is still included in the original story below. The company has also changed its FAQ for the event, which previously said that participants were required to use AI. Now, Epic says, "you can use as little or as much AI as you want." Original story: Not content with the humiliation it has already received over the vibe coded Epic Games Launcher beta , Epic is keen to pay a whole lot of money to aspiring vibe coders in an AI-focused game jam. The company is promising $65,000 worth of cash prizes and potential $50,000 grants for "standout" projects – assuming, of course, that you can stomach being part of Epic's attempted AI redemption tour. The 2026 AI MegaJam will take place from November 12 through 15, with registration open on Itch.io , challenging participants to build games using Unreal Engine or UEFN. The basic rules are roughly the same as normal game jams, which challenge indie devs to create fun, functional, small games under tight time constraints. It's a well-worn process that's created the prototypes for indie classics like Celeste, Don't Starve, and The Binding of Isaac. But the key difference here is that Epic really wants participants to use AI. "Bring any AI tools into your workflow, from asset generation to coding agents. Get creative! Prototype the mechanic you never had time for, or try the art style you weren’t sure you could pull off," the company says in its announcement . Cash prizes will be awarded in a number of categories, including $2,500 awards for the "best dev log showing how you used AI tools to build your game" and the best game using LLM-driven NPCs with AI conversations. For games Epic particularly likes, it's also offering "development continuation grants of up to $50,000 to keep building after the jam." Vibe your way to 50K. The 2026 Epic AI MegaJam begins Nov 12: https://t.co/aAXEqj7zmE https://t.co/h3Kgs9Y5zH October 22, 2026 With six-fingered promo art for the event and a tagline of "vibe your way to 50K," Epic's clearly poking fun at AI critics, but it's not really clear who's laughing. The responses on Twitter certainly aren't kind, and general pushback from devs on AI has been loud and consistent for some time. Certainly, Epic boss Tim Sweeney is happy to publicly feud with AI haters , and at least one former Fortnite producer says the anti-AI backlash is "mostly for show." But Epic's been fighting a losing battle for consumer goodwill ever since the Epic Games Store started its long, ineffectual war against Steam, and the company's "huge pivot" to AI doesn't seem to be endearing it to gamers, either. If the intent is to make people go "wow, look how quickly AI can make games," then I'm not sure how it's meant to be different from a normal game jam, where devs have been creating incredible projects for decades under similar time constraints without AI assistance. Right now, the number of games I could potentially play is somewhere between 100,000 and infinity. Every day, dozens of new games launch across digital stores, and every day, I learn of a cool retro title I could go back and play on classic hardware. At this point, I'm practically begging every new game I come across to give me a reason not to play it, and so far AI-driven development has been a very handy line in the sand.
